title: Nvidia Sell-Off: You Won’t Believe How Cheap the Stock Is - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia's stock is the cheapest it has been since the financial crisis Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) stock has had a busy few weeks. It was heavily affected by the resignation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, and questions are now surfacing about how much of Nvidia's sales were conducted legally and whether any of its chips ended up in China. Huang is now back as CEO, but there is no definitive answer on export issues, and the market isn't sticking around to find out the conclusion of this saga. Instead, it has sold off Nvidia's stock to a point not seen in years. In fact, with its stock closing at about $125 per share on Friday, it's traded at a price not seen since May 2025. After Huang returned, the stock rose to around $155 per share. Nvidia stock hasn’t been priced this low since mid-2025. However, Nvidia has grown significantly as a company since then, making its valuation cheap. But just how cheap is it? Let's take a look. First, let's look at how Nvidia is trading based on trailing earnings. For reference, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) trades at 20.3 times trailing earnings. As of the price Nvidia closed at on Nov. 24, the stock trades at just 16.7 times earnings. That type of discount is normally reserved for companies with major business problems or those operating in deeply cyclical industries. While Nvidia may operate in a cyclical industry, the reality is that the artificial intelligence build-out isn't wrapping up anytime soon, and there will always be a need to replace outdated or burnt-out equipment. However, the trailing price-to-earnings ratio is a bad metric for Nvidia. Why? It's all due to the growth Nvidia will produce. During the company’s fiscal third quarter of 2027 (ending Oct. 25), CFO Colette Kress raised the company’s revenue growth guidance for fiscal 2028 from 70% to 75%. That's an impressive figure considering how quickly Nvidia grew this year, and if those growth figures hold up, the stock will be even cheaper. Nvidia now trades for just 9.3 times next year's earnings. So, what's a fair value for Nvidia? If you think it's about 30 times trailing earnings, then if Nvidia rises to that level and hits next year's estimates, the stock could triple. A lot would need to go right with investigations, but it's not out of the question, either. While there are many unknowns about Nvidia's future, there are also many known factors. The AI boom isn't slowing down for anyone or anything, and that could lead to incredible performance over the next few years. I think now is the perfect time to buy Nvidia stock, as its price is driven more by fear than by reality. title: Anthropic’s Chip Choices Could Change the Nvidia Story. Here’s How. - The Motley Fool
content: Anthropic is spreading out its demand for AI accelerators across multiple companies. Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) made headlines recently because of its blockbuster IPO, and investors are still trying to decide how the newly public artificial intelligence (AI) company will impact the broader AI market. Some of the details Anthropic disclosed in its S-1 filing before going public shed light on its potential impact, especially on chip companies. Anthropic currently has deals with multiple chip companies to help provide the compute capacity it needs for its AI services. Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) is, unsurprisingly, a key supplier of chips to Anthropic, but so are Alphabet (GOOGL -2.13%) (GOOG -2.02%), Amazon (AMZN -3.12%), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -1.75%). Instead of tying itself to just one chip company, Anthropic has decided to spread out its chip vendors. That could change Nvidia's growth narrative in the coming years. Here's how it's shifting and why Nvidia investors don't need to panic just yet. Between cloud computing contracts and chip deals, Anthropic is on the hook for about $900 billion in spending over the next several years. That's a heck of a lot of money to spend, and Anthropic hopes it will accelerate its sales far beyond the company's current annual revenue run rate of $81 billion. It's also far too much money to funnel toward just one or two AI infrastructure companies. To minimize its supply chain risks, ensure it has the most advanced technology, and negotiate better chip prices, Anthropic spreads its chip deals across four key players. While Anthropic doesn't disclose all the details of each deal, including how much they might be worth, this data shows that Anthropic is clearly hedging its bets when it comes to buying AI chips. Nvidia's GPUs are still among the most in-demand chips in the world, and they're very likely to remain so for years to come due to AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia had an estimated 80%-90% market share of AI accelerators last year and is estimated to have 75% this year. That's both good and bad news for Nvidia. Having three-quarters of the AI accelerator market is huge, and it's part of the reason why Nvidia just reported another impressive quarter, with Q3 fiscal 2027 revenue rising 103% to $115.8 billion and earnings per share jumping 111% to $2.68. But AMD's GPUs and custom silicon from Google, Broadcom, and Amazon are reducing Nvidia's dominance. Part of the reason is that custom chips (like the ones Anthropic buys from Nvidia rivals) are good at handling agentic AI tasks and are more efficient than the raw processing power from GPUs. What's more, Nvidia's gross margins, while still high, are declining. The company said gross margins will be between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, down from nearly 75% in the third quarter. This downward pressure is mostly coming from rising memory costs right now, but intensifying chip competition could weigh on margins further in the coming years. Still, while Nvidia shareholders should be aware of how rival chip companies could impact the company over time, Nvidia is still the leading AI accelerator company. Its recent revenue guidance for 75% growth in the fourth quarter -- up from its previous guidance of 70% -- should reassure investors that the company isn't getting sidelined anytime soon. Michael Burry, the investor known for predicting the 2008 financial crisis, is sticking with his bearish view on Nvidia (NVDA). In a November 24 post on his Substack, Burry called the situation following Jensen Huang's return as president and CEO a "precarious normal." He also said his short thesis "is still valid, still has legs at full strength." At the same time, he disclosed buying more shares of Chinese companies JD.com (JD), Tencent (TCEHY), and BYD (BYDDF) as their share prices fell. Nvidia shares fell nearly 6% on Tuesday after surging 31% on Monday following news of Huang's return. However, Burry said his bearish view never depended on Huang leaving the company. The company has also faced pressure amid weakness in Chinese and Hong Kong stocks. At Tuesday's all-hands meeting, Huang defended Nvidia's management structure that has dozens of executives reporting directly to him. That gives senior leaders ready access to the founder, but it also concentrates decisions in one office. Nvidia's board had a fallback when Huang resigned earlier this month, naming CFO Colette Kress interim chief executive while it searched for a permanent replacement. For shareholders, the bigger question is who would have the authority to make long-term product and customer decisions if Huang left — or had to leave — again. His return restores continuity today, but his stance on succession gives investors little clarity about how a future handover would work. In his latest Substack, Burry also said that his bearish thesis never really depended on Huang's departure, so his reinstatement does little to change it. Burry's recent trading activity tells a more nuanced story, though. He sold most of his Nvidia puts and bought inexpensive, long-dated calls on Friday. According to the investor, he's still holding the calls as of Wednesday — and they have already doubled in value. However, if market optimism returns, Burry said he will short NVDA again at about $200 a share. That's roughly 41% above current levels, a gap that shows how much room he's willing to give a rebound before betting against the AI stock again. On the flip side, Wall Street analysts remain bullish as ever on NVDA stock heading into 2027. The consensus rating on Nvidia still sits at Strong Buy, with the mean price target of roughly $240 indicating potential upside of more than 65% from here. title: Why Nvidia Stock Is Falling Again - The Motley Fool
content: The cost of insuring debt across the AI trade just hit record highs. Nvidia Corporation (NVDA -3.91%) stock is down 5.4% as of 1:29 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25, as the sell-off in AI stocks deepens on worries over inflation and debt. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite are down 0.5% and 1.3%, respectively. Over the past two trading sessions, credit default swap (CDS) spreads -- basically the price of insurance on a company's debt going bad -- hit record highs for companies across the AI trade: from Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) and Oracle (ORCL -5.13%), to SpaceX (SPCX +1.30%) and CoreWeave (CRWV -0.08%). That last name, a neocloud whose business model is dependent on borrowing, saw its spread reach 1,314 basis points -- in other words, it would cost someone roughly $131,400 a year to insure $1 million in the company's debt. And in still more plain terms: that implies a roughly 68% chance of default within five years. These are some of Nvidia's biggest customers. If debt investors -- often regarded as the smartest on Wall Street -- are pricing in this sort of risk, it's fair for equity investors to question Nvidia's share price, even after its 40% fall over the last seven weeks. Of course, this morning's latest inflation numbers aren't helping calm anyone's nerves: October's Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index reading came in at 3.8%, well above the Fed's 2% goal. Nvidia investors and the market in general reacted positively to news of the return of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry leader, who has been endorsed by none other than President Donald Trump himself. Yet, the legal troubles are far from over for the most famous leather jacket-clad executive in the world right now, specifically in Nvidia's home state of California. The Attorney General for the state of California recently revealed that Nvidia may be facing charges over possible violations of U.S. chip export rules. Announcing an investigation into the company, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said, "The basic legal framework that we're looking at is the prohibitions in California law — both civil and criminal — against misleading investors and the public. As the excitement around Huang's return eventually dies down, investors should realize that the legal overhang around NVDA stock will continue to linger for a while. The company both directly and indirectly faces a number of investigations and inquiries involving federal agencies, national security matters, and congressional oversight. Last week, the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. Department of Justice confirmed an investigation into Megaspeed that began in 2024 after authorities identified suspicious activity involving potential semiconductor diversion. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, but that reportedly did not stop the company from acquiring Nvidia chips after the fact. Meanwhile, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is reportedly investigating Nvidia's accounting amid concerns involving financing arrangements with AI customers and whether those arrangements could obscure revenue quality and financial exposure. Reportedly, the DOJ is also reviewing Nvidia's acquisitions, sales practices, customer pressure, and the possible tying of AI chips to networking equipment. Reporting on the matter has also referenced Nvidia's Hugging Face deal and Groq technology agreement. Finally, Congressional scrutiny is inevitable for Jensen Huang, who has agreed to appear before numerous House committees on Dec. 1. Notably, the political situation could also become considerably more difficult for Nvidia once Democrats take control of Congress in January. Remove all these legal tangles from Nvidia's fundamentals, however, and the financials appear as healthy as ever. Nvidia delivered another clean double beat and guidance that topped expectations in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. CFO Colette Kress also increased the company's revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2028 to 75% from the prior 70%. Revenue totaled $115.8 billion in Q3, marking a 103% increase from the year-ago period and exceeding consensus estimates. title: Jensen Huang Says Nvidia's Next-Gen Vera Rubin Chips Will Generate $40 Billion in Revenue per Gigawatt, Up From $25 Billion for Grace Blackwell. What That Means for NVDA's Growth Runway. - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia isn't just achieving higher revenue per gigawatt through increased GPU selling prices. It's been an incredibly wild month for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) shareholders. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang and related dynamics kicked off a surge in selling action that saw the company's share price retreat 48% from the all-time high reached in early October. On Nov. 23, news that Huang had been reinstated as the CEO caused the company's share price to skyrocket 31.5% in a single trading session. The gains added nearly $1 trillion to the company's market capitalization, marking the largest single-day valuation gain for a company in history and spurring a wave of buying across the stock market that saw U.S. stocks rise by roughly $3 trillion. While Huang's return to Nvidia and the controversies over the smuggling of the company's export-banned chips to China will continue to be heavily discussed and debated in the near term, investors' focus will likely shift back to the company's actual business performance. Along those lines, Huang's estimates for the jump in monetization from the company's next-generation Vera Rubin processing platform look poised to play a powerful role in driving growth. After generating roughly $25 billion in revenue per gigawatt of compute with its Grace Blackwell platform, Huang sees the Vera Rubin platform generating $40 billion in sales per gigawatt -- good for a 60% increase. In addition to securing more revenue per gigawatt, Nvidia and its shareholders can also bet on a meaningful increase in the number of gigawatts of artificial intelligence (AI) compute as the data center build-out continues at a rapid pace. According to an estimate from Morgan Stanley, a Vera Rubin VR200 rack will set customers back roughly $7.8 million -- up from roughly $3.99 million for the GB300 rack. Other estimates suggest a lower price increase for the more capable, more energy-efficient racks, but more advanced processors and higher memory content are clearly set to facilitate substantial pricing and sales increases. On the other hand, more advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) and a greater number of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips aren't the only factors behind Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform delivering a big jump in sales per gigawatt compared to Blackwell. The company is also achieving the growth through its related Vera central processing units (CPUs) and new, internally developed networking hardware in its next-generation racks. Nvidia is seeing rapid growth in the CPU space and strong demand for Vera, and it expects that its total revenue from CPUs will more than double next year. The overall Vera Rubin platform provides a leap that bolsters Nvidia's edge in the AI compute space. In addition to simply generating more revenue per gigawatt, the performance jump provided by its newest GPUs and dramatic market share gains in the CPU category look poised to further strengthen the company's competitive position in the AI infrastructure market. As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Congress hearing looms, President Donald Trump has said his government could potentially pardon him if he is indicted, while adding that he didn't think such an act would be necessary. The President even said he has thought about having the U.S. government take a stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, saying "it's probably not too late," according to comments made to the New York Post. NVDA stock rallied 31.5% the same day, but the rally lost steam. Shares dipped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session and another 2.2% in overnight trading. While Huang's return as Nvidia chief is a major shot in the arm for the company and the broader AI trade, some commentators say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet. On Dec. 1, Huang will appear for a closed-door meeting with the House Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence committees on topics including his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and his company's security protocols. He will testify before the Senate Banking Committee later that week.
